title: The British-Indian Invasion: Michelin-Starred Gymkhana and Cult-Favourite Dishoom Set Sights on America
excerpt: London's two most celebrated Indian dining brands are crossing the Atlantic simultaneously — one with simmer sauces in every Whole Foods, the other with a Manhattan debut backed by LVMH.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Gymkhana and Dishoom are launching in the US, marking a historic Indian dining expansion.
  • Gymkhana Fine Foods introduces simmer sauces in Whole Foods, backed by $8.5 million funding.
  • Dishoom plans to open its first US location in NYC, valued at £300 million by LVMH.
  • 20,000 people waited for Dishoom's pop-up, highlighting demand for Indian cuisine in America.
  • These brands signify a shift in Indian food from niche to luxury in the US market.

Two of London's most iconic Indian restaurant empires are making their American moves at the same time — and together, they represent the biggest cross-border bet on Indian dining in US history. Gymkhana Fine Foods, the consumer-packaged-goods arm of the Michelin-starred Gymkhana restaurant, has just launched a line of simmer sauces and marinades in Whole Foods Markets nationwide. Dishoom, Britain's most beloved Indian cafe chain, is preparing to open its first American location in New York City this year, backed by a £300 million valuation from LVMH-linked private equity firm L Catterton. For India's global diaspora, the message is unmistakable: Indian cuisine is no longer a niche proposition. It's a luxury export. ## From the Tandoor to the Grocery Aisle Gymkhana Fine Foods marks the first time a Michelin-starred Indian restaurant has launched a consumer packaged goods line in the United States. The brand is backed by an $8.5 million Series A funding round led by CAVU Consumer Partners, founded by Rohan Oza — the investor and "Shark Tank" judge who helped build Vitaminwater, Smartwater, and Bai into household names. "Each sauce, marinade and chutney has been created to deliver the same bold, authentic flavors found in our restaurants," said Karam Sethi, culinary and creative director of JKS Restaurants, the family behind Gymkhana. "As we expand into the U.S., from our first restaurant in Las Vegas in 2025 to the launch of Gymkhana Fine Foods across the country, our aim remains the same: to offer Indian cuisine in its purest form." > **""There are so many young professionals, second-generation, third-generation people running businesses," Kavi Thakrar told the New York Times."** JKS Restaurants, founded by siblings Jyotin, Karam and Sunaina Sethi, now operates more than 30 concepts across London, including Trishna, Brigadiers, BiBi, and the recently opened Ambassadors Clubhouse in New York. Across the group, JKS boasts eight Michelin stars and six Bib Gourmand mentions — a staggering portfolio that makes it one of the most decorated Indian restaurant groups in the world. The CPG play is co-founded with Gulrez Arora, who grew the retail line in the UK first. It's a strategy that echoes what Italian fine dining did a generation ago — making restaurant-quality sauces accessible in the home kitchen. ## 20,000 on the Waitlist Meanwhile, Dishoom's American ambitions are even more dramatic. The chain, founded in 2010 by cousins Shamil and Kavi Thakrar and inspired by the vanishing Irani cafes of old Bombay, has grown into a cultural institution in Britain. It now operates 12 restaurants across the UK, serving more than 100,000 diners a week with a menu anchored by its legendary black dal, bacon naan rolls, and ruby chicken curry. In the summer of 2024, Dishoom ran a 10-day breakfast pop-up at Pastis in New York's Meatpacking District. It served roughly 7,000 people — and put 20,000 more on a waitlist. Reservations sold out in under five minutes. "There are so many young professionals, second-generation, third-generation people running businesses," Kavi Thakrar told the New York Times. "Indian food is finally part of the city's fabric." The LVMH connection gives Dishoom a powerful institutional endorsement. L Catterton, which has backed brands including Birkenstock and Ganni, typically invests in mid-market consumer businesses with luxury positioning and global growth potential. Dishoom plans to open two to three US sites per year, starting in lower Manhattan. The company has even begun experimenting with overnight rooms in Notting Hill — testing a possible Dishoom hotel concept. ## A Signal for the Entire Industry

The significance of both moves goes beyond the brands themselves. When Rohan Oza — the man who made coconut water mainstream — puts $8.5 million behind Indian simmer sauces, it signals that institutional capital sees Indian cuisine as the next major consumer category. When LVMH's investment arm values an Indian cafe chain at £300 million, it elevates the entire sector. Indian cuisine is having what industry observers call its "moment." Concepts across the US are innovating with modern versions of traditional dishes, and investors are paying attention. Just last year, fast-casual chains like Curry Up Now and Rasa secured funding to fuel national expansion. At the grocery level, brands like Truly Indian have picked up NEXTY Awards at Natural Products Expo West. ## Why It Matters for NRIs For the Indian diaspora in America, the simultaneous arrival of Gymkhana and Dishoom marks a generational shift. These are not immigrants adapting their cuisine for Western palates — they are global brands bringing Indian food on their own terms, backed by some of the world's most powerful investors. The next time an NRI in New York craves bacon naan rolls or wants to cook a Michelin-quality lamb rogan josh at home, they will not need to ask a relative visiting from London to smuggle it in. It will be on the shelf at Whole Foods — or around the corner in Manhattan. ## What's Next Gymkhana's restaurant at the Aria Resort and Casino in Las Vegas continues to anchor the group's US presence, while the CPG line aims for national grocery distribution beyond Whole Foods. Dishoom's exact Manhattan address and opening date remain under wraps, but industry sources point to late 2026. The Thakrars have said they are focused on "deepening hospitality" over rapid scale — a deliberate contrast to fast-casual expansion plays. Together, these two brands represent a new playbook: British-incubated, Indian-rooted, American-scaled. The invasion has begun.
